topic.title: JavaScript — Quick Revision
topic.subtitle: The questions that come up in almost every JavaScript interview.

questions.q: What is the difference between var, let and const?

items: **var** is function-scoped, hoisted and initialised as `undefined`; it can be redeclared.
**let** is block-scoped, hoisted but unusable until its declaration (temporal dead zone); it can be reassigned.
**const** is block-scoped like let, but the binding cannot be reassigned. Objects it points to can still be mutated.

questions.q: What is a closure? Give a practical use.

answer.value: A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished executing.
Common uses: data privacy, function factories, memoisation, debounce/throttle and event handlers that need remembered state.

questions.q: How does this work in JavaScript?

answer.value: `this` is decided by **how a function is called**, not where it is written:

items: Method call `obj.fn()` → `this` is `obj`.
Plain call `fn()` → `undefined` in strict mode (global object otherwise).
`call`, `apply`, `bind` set `this` explicitly.
`new Fn()` → the newly created object.
Arrow functions have no own `this`; they use the one from the enclosing scope.

questions.q: Explain the event loop, microtasks and macrotasks.

answer.value: JavaScript runs on one thread. The call stack executes synchronous code; async work is handed to the browser/Node and its callback is queued. When the stack is empty the event loop picks the next task.

items: **Microtasks** (Promise `.then`, `queueMicrotask`) run to completion after the current task, before anything else.
**Macrotasks** (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O, UI events) run one per loop turn.

answer.value: Declarations are registered during the creation phase of an execution context, so they can be referenced before the line that declares them. Function declarations are fully hoisted; `var` is hoisted as `undefined`; `let`/`const`/`class` are hoisted but stay in the temporal dead zone until declared.

questions.q: How do Promises work and what is async/await?

answer.value: A Promise represents a value that will exist later. It is **pending**, then settles as **fulfilled** or **rejected**. `then/catch/finally` chain follow-up work. `async/await` is syntax on top of promises that makes asynchronous code read top to bottom.
`await` pauses only the async function, not the whole thread. Independent calls should run together with `Promise.all`.

`===` compares value and type with no conversion. `==` converts operands first (type coercion), which gives surprising results such as `0 == ''` and `null == undefined`. Prefer `===`; use `Object.is` when you need to tell `NaN` and `-0` apart.

'5' == 5;   // true
'5' === 5;  // false
null == undefined;  // true
null === undefined; // false
NaN === NaN; // false

Every object has an internal link ([[Prototype]]) to another object. When a property isn't found on the object, the engine walks up this chain until it finds it or reaches `null`. `class` syntax is sugar over this mechanism.

questions.q: map vs forEach vs filter vs reduce?

items: `forEach` runs a function for each item and returns `undefined`.
`map` returns a new array of transformed items.
`filter` returns a new array of items that pass a test.
`reduce` folds the array into a single value (number, object, array…).

questions.q: call, apply and bind — what is the difference?

items: `fn.call(ctx, a, b)` invokes immediately with arguments listed.
`fn.apply(ctx, [a, b])` invokes immediately with an array of arguments.
`fn.bind(ctx, a)` returns a **new function** with `this` (and optional leading args) fixed.

questions.q: Shallow copy vs deep copy — how do you clone an object?

answer.value: A shallow copy duplicates only the top level; nested objects stay shared. Spread (`{...o}`) and `Object.assign` are shallow. For a deep copy use `structuredClone(o)` (handles dates, maps, sets, cycles). `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(o))` works only for plain JSON data and drops functions, `undefined` and dates.

items: **Debounce** waits until calls stop for N ms, then runs once (search-as-you-type).
**Throttle** runs at most once every N ms (scroll, resize).

questions.q: What are arrow functions and how do they differ from normal functions?

items: Shorter syntax; implicit return for expressions.
No own `this`, `arguments` or `super` — they use the enclosing ones.
Cannot be used with `new` and have no `prototype`.

questions.q: What is event delegation and bubbling?

answer.value: Events travel from the target up through its ancestors (**bubbling**). With delegation you attach one listener to a parent and inspect `event.target`, instead of attaching one per child — fewer listeners and it works for elements added later.

questions.q: What are the primitive types in JavaScript?

answer.value: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null` and `symbol`. Everything else is an object. Primitives are immutable and compared by value; objects are compared by reference. Note `typeof null === 'object'` is a long-standing quirk.

questions.q: What is destructuring, spread and rest?

answer.value:
const { name, age = 18, ...others } = user;   // object destructuring + rest
const [first, , third] = list;             // array destructuring
const merged = { ...a, ...b };             // spread
function sum(...nums) {}                   // rest parameters

An iterator is any object with a `next()` method returning `{ value, done }`. A generator function (`function*`) produces an iterator whose body can pause at `yield` and resume later — useful for lazy sequences and custom iteration.

items: **Currying** turns `f(a, b)` into `f(a)(b)`, enabling partial application.
**Memoisation** caches results by arguments so repeated calls are instant.
